samples.summary: DOCX export still interpolates attacker-controllable color strings into XML attributes unescaped, while the same function's headingLevel sink was hardened
samples.evidence:
This change hardened `headingLevel` at docx-style-map.ts:102 because "a string could otherwise close the quote and inject attributes", but the two sibling sinks in the same function are untouched: line 73 `parts.push(`<w:color w:val="${colorHex.replace('#','')}"/>`)` and line 77 `w:fill="${bgHex.replace('#','')}"`. `colorHex` comes from `defaultColorResolver`, which returns the stored value verbatim for the `string` and `{kind:'srgb'}` forms (model/color.ts:16-17) — no hex validation, and `<`, `>`, `"` are not escaped (`escapeXmlAttr` is applied only to fontFamily).

Two untrusted sources reach it, one of them the very path this diff set out to validate:
(a) the internal clipboard payload — the new sanitizer's `asStoredColor` returns any string as-is (`if (typeof value === 'string') return value;`, clipboard.ts:91) and accepts any string as an srgb `value` (clipboard.ts:94), so a hostile page's `application/x-waffledocs` payload with `style.color = 'FF0000"/><w:fldSimple w:instr=" DDEAUTO c:\\windows\\system32\\cmd.exe "/><w:color w:val="000000'` survives sanitization verbatim;
(b) DOCX import, which builds `style.color = `#${val}`` from an attacker-supplied `w:color/@w:val` with no validation (packages/docs/src/import/docx-style-map.ts:62, and `#${color}` for borders at :264).
The value then lands unescaped in `word/document.xml`, allowing arbitrary OOXML element injection (field codes such as DDEAUTO / INCLUDEPICTURE for command execution or NTLM leakage) into a .docx the victim exports and typically forwards — or, minimally, a corrupt file Word refuses to open.

That this is an oversight rather than an accepted risk is visible in the sibling exporters, which do validate the same value: `pdf-style-map.ts:146` gates on `/^#?([0-9a-f]{6})$/i` and slides' PPTX writer escapes it (`escapeXmlAttr(c.value...)`, packages/slides/src/export/pptx/color.ts:35). Fix: run colors through `escapeXmlAttr` and/or a `^#?[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$` check on both the export side and in `asStoredColor`.

samples.summary: Table-cell backgroundColor from a clipboard payload is interpolated unescaped into <w:shd w:fill> in the exported DOCX
samples.evidence: `docx-exporter.ts:309-311` does `const hex = cell.style.backgroundColor.replace('#','')` and interpolates it straight into `<w:shd w:val="clear" w:color="auto" w:fill="${hex}"/>` — no escaping, no hex validation. The newly added sanitizer accepts any string here: `sanitizeCellStyle` does `const backgroundColor = asString(value.backgroundColor); if (...) style.backgroundColor = backgroundColor;` (packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:217-218), and the `tableCells` half of the payload goes through the same function (clipboard.ts:355). Border colors take the same shape (`sanitizeBorder`, clipboard.ts:209) and DOCX import also produces `#${color}` unchecked (import/docx-style-map.ts:264). Attacker: hostile page puts a `application/x-waffledocs` payload on the clipboard with a table cell whose `backgroundColor` is `FFFFFF"/><w:injected …/><w:shd w:fill="FFFFFF`; the victim pastes and exports, producing attacker-chosen XML inside word/document.xml.

samples.summary: BlockStyle.alignment is interpolated unescaped into <w:jc w:val="…"> and is read back from Yorkie tree attributes with an unchecked cast
samples.evidence: `buildParagraphPropertiesXml` interpolates the alignment verbatim: `parts.push(`<w:jc w:val="${align}"/>`)` (docx-style-map.ts:106-109). The clipboard path now allowlists it (`asOneOf(value.alignment, ALIGNMENTS)`, clipboard.ts:181), but the CRDT read path does not: `packages/frontend/src/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.ts:222` does `if ('alignment' in attrs) partial.alignment = attrs.alignment as BlockStyle['alignment'];` — a raw string cast from tree node attributes. A participant able to write raw Yorkie tree attributes for a shared document (edit-permission collaborator issuing a crafted update rather than using the UI) can therefore set `alignment` to `left"/><w:fldSimple w:instr="…"/><w:jc w:val="left` and inject XML/field codes into every other user's exported .docx. The canvas renderer only string-compares alignment, so nothing else rejects the value. I could not confirm a concrete non-UI write path for tree attrs, hence low confidence; the unescaped sink and the unchecked cast are both directly observable.

samples.summary: The slides element clipboard still casts an attacker-writable clipboard payload straight to Element[] (which carries docs Block[]), bypassing the new docs sanitizer
samples.evidence: The threat model this change introduces — "the `WAFFLEDOCS_MIME` flavour is JSON that *any* page can put on the system clipboard … casting it to `Block[]` would let a hostile page write arbitrary values straight into the shared Yorkie tree, the renderer, and the DOCX/PDF exporters" (packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:36-43) — applies verbatim to the slides clipboard, which is not fixed. `deserializeElements` validates only `magic` and `Array.isArray(elements)` and then `return parsed.elements;` (slides/.../clipboard.ts:45-48), with the MIME `web application/x-wafflebase-slides+json` — a web custom format any page can write via `navigator.clipboard.write`. `Element` embeds docs blocks (`packages/slides/src/model/element.ts:1` imports `Block` from `@wafflebase/docs`, `:265 blocks: Block[]`), so a hostile payload's arbitrary `headingLevel`, `style.color`, `image.src`, unknown block types and junk keys reach the docs model, renderer and exporters through the slides paste path while the docs paste path is now validated. An added-but-bypassable validation reads as covered; at minimum the slides deserializer should reuse the docs sanitizer for the `blocks` of each text-bearing element.

samples.summary: Sanitizer accepts any string as image.src, which is later fetched cross-origin with credentials during export
samples.evidence: `sanitizeImageData` only type-checks the src (`const src = asString(value.src)`, clipboard.ts:112) — no scheme or host allowlist, unlike `href`, which every consumer gates with `isSafeUrl` (text-editor.ts:1372, :1699; pdf-painter.ts:834; docs-link-popover.tsx:183). A pasted/collaborator-supplied `image.src` is passed to the export image fetcher, which is credentialed and accepts absolute URLs untouched: `resolveImageUrl` returns any absolute URL verbatim (`if (/^[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*:/i.test(url)) return url;`, packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:15) and `docsImageFetcher` does `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` (export-utils.ts:51). So a hostile clipboard payload (or a pasted block that lands in a shared doc) causes every exporting collaborator's browser to issue a credentialed request to an attacker-chosen URL — a tracking/CSRF beacon — and lets internal/same-origin endpoint responses be embedded as "images" in the exported file. Recommend a scheme allowlist (http/https/data/blob) on `src` in the sanitizer, and dropping `credentials: 'include'` for non-backend origins.

samples.summary: New validator clamps headingLevel/listLevel but leaves every other numeric field unbounded, so a hostile payload can write extreme geometry into the shared CRDT
samples.evidence: `asNumber` only rejects non-finite values (clipboard.ts:69-71). Block style numbers (`lineHeight`, `marginTop/Bottom`, `textIndent`, `marginLeft` — clipboard.ts:183-189), image geometry (`width`/`height`/`rotation`/crops — clipboard.ts:113-126), and `colSpan`/`rowSpan` (`Math.trunc(colSpan)` with only a `> 1` test — clipboard.ts:238-241) accept values like `1e300`, while `headingLevel` and `listLevel` are clamped. Those values are written into the shared Yorkie document by the paste path, so a single hostile clipboard payload can persist geometry that drives the layout/pagination loops (and the DOCX `pxToTwips`/`gridSpan` writers) for every collaborator who later opens the document — a persistent client-side DoS rather than a one-off local glitch. Array lengths (blocks, rows, cells) are likewise uncapped. Clamping these to the same ranges the UI enforces would make the validator's "each value shape-checked" claim (clipboard.ts:43) actually hold.

verdict.reason: Verified every link in the chain. The unescaped sinks are present exactly as quoted: docx-style-map.ts:73 interpolates `colorHex.replace('#','')` into `<w:color w:val="...">` and :77 does the same for `w:fill`, while escapeXmlAttr (defined :25) is applied only to font family (:53-54). `.replace('#','')` removes one hash and does not neutralize `"`, `<` or `>`. No upstream validation exists: defaultColorResolver returns raw strings (model/color.ts:16) and raw srgb values (:17). Both claimed untrusted sources are real — asStoredColor returns any string verbatim (view/clipboard.ts:91) and accepts any string as an srgb value (:94-95), reaching style.color/backgroundColor via sanitizeInlineStyle (:154-157) on the documented-untrusted application/x-waffledocs payload (clipboard.ts:378; docs/design/docs/docs.md:226 explicitly calls that payload untrusted); and DOCX import builds `#${val}` from attacker-supplied w:color/@w:val with no validation (import/docx-style-map.ts:62, and shd/@fill at :76). The sink is reachable on the live export path: docx-exporter.ts:217 calls buildRunPropertiesXml(inline.style) and splices the result raw into <w:r> at :222 (it escapes inline.text at :218-221 but not the attribute path). The asymmetry is confirmed too: headingLevel in the same function is coerced at :102, and the sibling PDF exporter gates the same value on /^#?([0-9a-f]{6})$/i with a black fallback (pdf-style-map.ts:146-147), showing this is an oversight rather than accepted risk. verdict.reason: The claimed code is present verbatim. docx-exporter.ts:309-311 interpolates cell.style.backgroundColor into the w:fill attribute after only stripping the first '#' — no hex validation and no XML attribute escaping. The value is unconstrained: sanitizeCellStyle (clipboard.ts:217-218) accepts any string via asString (clipboard.ts:65-67), and CellStyle.backgroundColor is typed as a bare string (model/types.ts:463-464). The payload is attacker-controlled and reachable: deserializeClipboard sanitizes payload.tableCells (clipboard.ts:355) with the same function, and text-editor.ts:1240-1246 reads the WAFFLEDOCS_MIME clipboard flavour, deserializes it, and applies data.tableCells to the document via pasteTableCells; the file's own comment (clipboard.ts:36-43) confirms any page can place this MIME type on the system clipboard and that handlePaste prefers it. No guard elsewhere makes it unreachable, and unsafe input handling into a structured-document sink is within the security lens's injection lane.

verdict.reason: Both halves of the claim are directly observable and unguarded. (1) docx-style-map.ts:106-109 interpolates style.alignment verbatim into the <w:jc w:val="..."/> attribute with no escaping or coercion, even though the same file defines escapeXmlAttr (25-32), applies it to fontFamily (53-56), and defensively clamps headingLevel (102) with a comment explicitly warning that untrusted values could close the quote and inject attributes. (2) yorkie-doc-store.ts:222 casts a raw CRDT tree attribute to BlockStyle['alignment'], and the only downstream "normalizer", normalizeBlockStyle (model/types.ts:280-282), is a bare spread over defaults that validates nothing — so no already-guarded refutation holds. The chain is reachable end-to-end: docs-export-button.tsx:47 exports editor.getStore().getDocument() -> docx-actions.ts:50 -> docx-exporter.ts:182 -> the sink, and getDocument() (yorkie-doc-store.ts:546-570) builds block styles via treeNodeToBlock -> parseBlockStyle from tree attributes (411/437). Sibling producers are allowlisted (clipboard.ts:181-182; import/docx-style-map.ts:104-107), confirming the CRDT read path is the one uncovered producer, and the renderer only string-compares alignment (layout.ts:890-910) so nothing else rejects a hostile value. An actor with write access to the shared Yorkie tree sets alignment to a string that closes the quote and injects elements/field codes into every other collaborator's exported .docx — template/XML injection from untrusted input, squarely in the injection lane.

finding.summary: Untrusted `headingLevel` is interpolated unescaped into a DOCX XML attribute; this change lengthens the taint path by making the value survive a list round trip
finding.evidence: `buildParagraphPropertiesXml` builds `<w:pStyle w:val="Heading${headingLevel}"/>` with no escaping or numeric validation, even though the same file defines `escapeXmlAttr` (docx-style-map.ts:25) whose comment warns the risk is that a value can "inject attributes". `headingLevel` is only typed as `1|2|...|6`; at runtime it can be any JSON value because `deserializeClipboard` (packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts:40-45) returns `payload.blocks as Block[]` unvalidated and `TextEditor.handlePaste` feeds it straight to `insertBlocks` (text-editor.ts:1228,1240). Attack: a hostile page sets the `application/x-wafflebase-docs` flavour on a copy event with a block whose `headingLevel` is the string `1"/><w:evil/><w:x w:val="`; the victim pastes, exports to DOCX, and injected WordprocessingML lands in `word/document.xml`. Before this change a pasted *list-item*'s level was destroyed (setBlockType deleted it and toggleList hardcoded 'paragraph'); now `pastedHeadingLevel` (text-editor.ts:41) forwards it, `MemDocStore.setBlockType` retains it for `list-item` (memory.ts:258-260), and `unlistedBlockType` re-applies it verbatim as the level of a real `heading` (types.ts:337-344), reaching the unescaped sink via `block.type === 'heading' ? block.headingLevel : undefined` (docx-exporter.ts:184). Fix: clamp/coerce the level to 1..6 at the model boundary, or escape at line 96.

verdict.reason: The finding claims buildParagraphPropertiesXml interpolates headingLevel directly into the pStyle attribute "with no escaping or numeric validation". The working tree does not contain that code. docx-style-map.ts:102 coerces and clamps before interpolation: `const level = Math.min(6, Math.max(1, Math.trunc(Number(headingLevel)) || 1));` and line 103 interpolates `level`, not `headingLevel`. The exact attacker payload cited in the finding passes through Number() to NaN, then `|| 1`, then the 1..6 clamp, so the emitted attribute value is always a primitive integer 1-6 — quote-breaking / attribute injection is unreachable regardless of what deserializeClipboard, pastedHeadingLevel, MemDocStore.setBlockType, or unlistedBlockType forward, so the upstream taint path is irrelevant. Grep confirms line 103 is the only pStyle/Heading interpolation in src/, reached solely from docx-exporter.ts:184, so there is no alternate unguarded sink. Tests at test/export/docx-style-map.test.ts:100-116 assert the exact hostile string is neutralized (no w:customStyle, emits Heading1) and that 42 / 2.7 / -3 clamp to Heading6 / Heading2 / Heading1. The remediation the finding prescribes ("clamp/coerce the level to 1..6") is already implemented at the sink.

finding.summary: No schema validation on the internal clipboard payload, so attacker-controlled block fields (including the now-retained `headingLevel`) become model state and are written into the shared CRDT
finding.evidence: `deserializeClipboard` only checks `version === 1` and `Array.isArray(payload.blocks)`, then returns `payload.blocks as Block[]` — an unchecked cast of attacker-supplied JSON (clipboard.ts:40-48). Any page can populate the custom `WAFFLEDOCS_MIME` flavour on a `copy` event, and `handlePaste` prefers that flavour over `text/html`/`text/plain` (text-editor.ts:1226-1244). With this change the pasted `headingLevel` is no longer dropped when the block is a list item, so a non-numeric or out-of-range value can be handed to `YorkieDocStore.setBlockType`, which stringifies it into the shared tree attribute (`attrs.headingLevel = String(opts?.headingLevel ?? 1)`, yorkie-doc-store.ts:1386) and persists it through the backend `docs-tree` serializer. Co-editors read it back via `Number(attrs.headingLevel)` (yorkie-doc-store.ts:439), yielding `NaN` — one user's paste can poison a block attribute for every collaborator and for the stored document. I could not confirm a memory-safety or code-execution consequence, only corrupted shared state plus the export-injection sink above, hence medium confidence. Recommend validating/normalizing pasted blocks (type enum, headingLevel in 1..6, list fields) in `deserializeClipboard` or `insertBlocks`.

verdict.reason:
The claimed absence is not real: `packages/docs/src/view/clipboard.ts` contains a full schema validator/normalizer for the untrusted internal clipboard payload, and `deserializeClipboard` uses it.

- `deserializeClipboard` (clipboard.ts:347-360) does NOT cast `payload.blocks as Block[]`. After the `version === 1` check it returns `{ blocks: sanitizeBlocks(payload.blocks), tableCells: sanitizeCellRows(payload.tableCells, 0) }`, with an inline comment stating both halves go through the same validation because the payload is attacker-reachable. `deserializeBlocks` (clipboard.ts:22-30) does the same.
- `sanitizeBlocks`/`sanitizeBlock` (clipboard.ts:280-332) rebuild the model from scratch: block `type` is constrained to the `BLOCK_TYPES` enum with a `paragraph` fallback (clipboard.ts:45-48, 282), ids are regenerated rather than trusted (285-286), inlines and styles are shape-checked, unknown keys are dropped.
- The specific `headingLevel` concern is explicitly handled: `asHeadingLevel` (clipboard.ts:84-88) requires a finite integer in 1..6 and otherwise returns undefined; headings fall back to `1` (307) and list-items only keep a remembered level if it validates (309-310). So a non-numeric or out-of-range pasted `headingLevel` can never reach `YorkieDocStore.setBlockType`, and `Number(attrs.headingLevel)` cannot become NaN via this path.
- List fields the finding asked for are also normalized: `listKind` via the `LIST_KINDS` enum and `listLevel` clamped to 0..MAX_LIST_LEVEL (clipboard.ts:312-317); table nesting is depth-bounded (MAX_TABLE_DEPTH, 59, 256).
- The paste entry point the finding cites does go through this validator: `text-editor.ts:1240-1242` reads `WAFFLEDOCS_MIME` and calls `deserializeClipboard(json)`.

One counterexample suffices, and here the entire mechanism the reviewer said was missing exists in the exact file named.
